articles.title_orig: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.title_zh: White House defends Trump comment to let Iran 'take out' LA and San Diego
articles.content_orig:
Trump on Iran: 'Let them take out LA, let them take out San Diego'
Donald Trump's remark that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego has sparked fierce backlash from California politicians - and a strongly worded rebuttal from the White House.
California Governor Gavin Newsom condemned the comment - made by Trump at a campaign rally in Nebraska - as  "deranged and dangerous," while LA Mayor Karen Bass described them as threats and an attempt to "encourage attacks on American lives".
According to the White House, however, Trump was saying that American cities would have been threatened by Iran had he not launched a war there earlier this year.
Both LA and San Diego house major US military installations including Navy ports and Air Force bases.
Trump, while speaking on Monday in Nebraska about the Iran conflict, said: "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe. They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles, let them take out San Diego."
There were cheers from sections of the audience as the comments about the two Californian cities were made.
The morning after Trump's statement, Governor Newsom announced that the "dangerous - if not treasonous" statement had prompted him to direct California's State Threat Assessment Center to "monitor the situation in the event that foreign actors interpret the remarks as an invitation" to target California.
The agency is designed to detect and prevent security threats in the state.
San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria wrote that the city was not collateral damage in a post on X, while demanding Trump keep it out of his "reckless war talk".
Trump is yet to respond to the statements made by California's leaders.
In a post on X, White House Communications Director Stephen Cheung described the "media freakout" over Trump's comments as "not rooted in reality".
"He was clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped," Cheung wrote. "America is safer because of the President. Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money".
The president and other administration officials often claim that disrupting Iran's nuclear programme was essential for US national security, and that any issues that have stemmed from the conflict were necessary.
A separate X post, from the official White House rapid response account, described journalists from the Los Angeles Times reporting on the comments as "buffoons" and again pushed back on the characterisation of the comments by Newsom and others.
"He was saying the US is fighting to STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego with a nuclear weapon â which they would if they had the chance," the account added.
San Diego, located 17 miles (27km) from the border with Mexico, is the eighth largest city in the US and is home to Naval Base San Diego, the home port of the US Navy's Pacific Fleet, and Naval Amphibious Base Coronado - the main training centre Navy Seals on the West Coast.
It is also where Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton is located, a base which 70,000 service members and civilians work at.
Located approximately 120 miles (193 KM) north of San Diego, Los Angeles is the second most populous city in the US.
It is home to the space system command headquarters of the US Space Force, as well as the Los Angeles Air Force Base.
Trump and Newsom met when the president visited California in January after the state was hit by wildfires
This not the first time the US president and California governor, who may run for president in 2028, have publicly clashed.
Last year Trump described him as incompetent, saying he had failed to adequately respond after some of the Los Angeles anti-immigration enforcement protests turned violent.
Newsom accused Trump of a "brazen abuse of power" after military personnel were deployed to secure federal buildings during those protests.
Earlier this year, Trump mocked Newsom's dyslexia, saying presidents should not have learning disabilities, which led to criticism from dyslexia charities.

articles.title_zh: S&P 500, Nasdaq on track for record closing highs as focus turns to earnings
articles.content_orig:
S&P tops 7,800 for first time in history as investors optimistic despite signs of instability in US economy
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at a record high after a rally around AI chipmakers and a dip in US treasury yields.
At market’s close, the S&P 500 was up 0.58%, topping 7,800 for the first time in its history. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 0.45%, while the Dow, which is slightly down from its record high in August, climbed 0.49%.
Investors appeared optimistic after recent developments for chipmakers including Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that showed growth in the markets for the chips used to power AI.
Wall Street has also grown more optimistic that the US Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its next board meeting in October. Job figures from September showed underwhelming growth in the labor market, and multiple Fed officials have said the next interest rate increase can probably wait.
The optimism in the stock market, largely coming from continuing investment in AI, has defied other signs of instability in the US economy and global politics.
The US bond market, typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, has been in turmoil in recent weeks. US bond yields, or the return an investor receives when a bond matures, reached recent highs amid concerns over high inflation and interest rates. The yield for 10-year US treasury bonds on Monday reached 5.349%, the highest since April 2022, before dipping back down on Tuesday.
For American consumers, higher energy prices continue to be a major pain point. While gas prices have dipped over the last week, prices are still about $1.20 a gallon on average higher than a year ago. Diesel, which is used to fuel trucks, buses and trains, has also gone down from record high but is still over 40% higher than a year ago.
The economy is expected to be a top issue in the upcoming midterm elections, with many voters expressing frustration over high prices. Donald Trump, who has been stumping for Republican candidates across the country, has been trying to paint a different picture for voters.
At a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump said that “our nation is doing better now than it’s ever done” and that gas prices would fall below $1.85 a gallon “in no time”.

No cases of plague have been identified among individuals who came into contact with a Siberian plague institute worker who died on Friday, according to Russia’s health watchdog on Tuesday.
In a statement, the monitoring body Rospotrebnadzor confirmed that no infectious illnesses had been reported among employees at the Irkutsk plague research facility over the past 10 days. Extensive medical testing further showed that no microorganisms connected to her professional duties were present in the deceased woman's body.
Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, stated that a hazardous diagnosis was not confirmed. She added that approximately 60 per cent of those under quarantine have now been released.
Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, was previously reported to have been exposed to the bacteria after she accidentally broke a test tube containing the pathogen while she was collecting samples, according to The Kyiv Independent.
She was hospitalised on 29 September with severe pneumonia of "unknown origin” and placed on a ventilator , but died shortly after.
Russian authorities further told the World Health Organization on Tuesday that it has no cases of plague in ⁠the city of Irkutsk in Siberia. The WHO has ‌previously said ​that the risk of ‌plague to the general ​population appeared to be low.
Moscow, which is required under global health rules to respond to WHO requests within 24 hours, previously told the WHO that authorities were investigating whether pneumonic plague caused her death.
"No ‌case of this dangerous disease has been recorded in the city of Irkutsk, Russian Federation," ‌Russian authorities said in an official ‌response to a WHO request, read out by WHO spokesperson Christian Lindmeier at a Geneva press briefing.
They also told the UN agency they have identified the people in contact with the deceased and that test results for dangerous infectious pathogens were negative.
Independent Russian outlet Lyudi Baikal reported that several hospitals in the city of Irkutsk had closed for a three-week quarantine.
At least 197 people suspected of having direct or indirect contact with the technician were placed under medical isolation, the newspaper reported. More than 100 of those individuals were being monitored in hospital wards.
Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia welcomed US President Donald Trump's offer of assistance to help following the worker’s death.
"It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters. He said the public health watchdog was handling the situation and would provide further information as it became available.
Trump on Monday described the situation as a "big problem for Russia".

Germany’s former foreign intelligence chief has been detained on suspicion of passing state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the country’s federal prosecutor’s office has said.
Prosecutors allege August Hanning, whose tenure at the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) ended in 2005, paid for access to classified documents from a former aide at the BND. It is claimed Hanning used them to prepare an analysis which he intended to sell on to a foreign intelligence service as part of his consulting activities.
He is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason and espionage”, the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
Prosecutors did not identify which foreign intelligence service he was allegedly preparing the analysis for, and it ⁠was not immediately clear whether it reached its intended recipient.
According to German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung the case does not ⁠involve Russia.
Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Tölz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany on Tuesday. The former aide, ‌identified only as Manfred D, was also arrested on Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany.
Manfred D is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Prosecutors said they are also searching the suspects’ premises in these locations and in Berlin.
From the spring of 2010 until July 2022, Manfred D continuously obtained valuable information for Hanning from the BND in exchange for payment, said the prosecutor’s statement.
He allegedly provided him with nearly 2,000 documents, many of them classified and intended solely for internal use within the BND and senior-level intelligence ‌briefings at the chancellery.
According to the statement, Hanning was in close contact with a member of another state intelligence service, and he supplied this individual with political information over several years, which was partly based on material he had received from Manfred D.
Hanning was president of the BND from December 1998 to November 2005. Manfred D served as his chief of staff at that time, and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.
“In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor's office said.
The German newspaper Bild said that the investigation was launched after the discovery of an alleged leak of intelligence reports intended for the chancellery.
The arrests came after a separate investigation into allegations that Hanning abducted Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years.
The current investigation stems from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated.
Both of the accused will be brought before the investigating judge of the Federal Court of Justice on Tuesday and Wednesday.
German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz voiced his shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation.
“This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services.
“We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations levelled against former BND chief Hanning,” von Notz told Spiegel Online.

Agents arrested August Hanning (pictured from 2015) at his home on Tuesday
Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.
Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.
Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.
Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.
Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near MÃ¼nster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.
Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".
"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.
"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".
Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".
Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.
Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.
State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.
It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.

A California couple has been arrested on child abuse charges after an investigation into a surrogacy scheme involving at least 21 children ranging in age from a few months to 13 years, authorities said Tuesday.
Guojun Xuan, 66, and his wife, Silvia Zhang, 39, face several counts of child abuse, as well as conspiracy to commit child abuse, accessory after the fact, and dissuading a witness, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman said.
“This case is unprecedented. It is horrific,” Hochman said during a news conference Tuesday morning. “The physical abuse, beating and punishment that these very young children received is despicable.”
Prosecutors are seeking $100 million bail for the couple because of the serious nature of the charges and because they are flight risks, Hochman said. They were scheduled to be arraigned at the Pasadena courthouse later Tuesday.
Fifteen children were removed from the couple’s opulent home in Arcadia last year after an allegation of abuse, and another six living elsewhere were also located. They ranged in age from 2 months to 13 years, with most between 1 and 3. Police believe Zhang gave birth to one or two of the children while the rest were carried and delivered by surrogates.
Hochman said the couple set up a surrogacy agency that they operated from their home and used that agency to hire surrogates throughout the U.S.
“The house could only be described as a house of horrors for these incredible young children,” Hochman said.
Zhang and Xuan were first arrested in May 2025 after a hospital reported that their 2-month-old infant had a traumatic head injury, the result of a nanny at the home violently shaking the baby, according to Arcadia police.
Arcadia police did not file charges at the time, saying they needed to complete the investigation.
Hochman said the couple set up three rooms they called learning centers, where the children spent several hours a day sitting at desks under the supervision of nannies.
Through an extensive surveillance system including motion-activated cameras, the couple watched as the nannies subjected the children to physical abuse including daily beatings, he said.
In one video, Xuan enters one of the rooms and tells a nanny to strike a child harder, and in another he joins the nanny in hitting the child, Hochman said.
He said the nannies were told “not to leave any physical marks on the children,” and when police arrived to investigate in May 2025, the couple told the children to deny they had been beaten.
After examining the surveillance footage, police issued an arrest warrant for Chunmei Li, the nanny seen hurting the 2-month-old infant, but she could not be found.
Hochman said “there will be a reckoning” for the defendants, one of whom faces more than 17 years in prison if convicted.
When asked about the couple’s motivation, Hochman said that was part of the ongoing investigation, as was the parentage of each child.
Mitchell Krems, Xuan’s attorney, previously told ABC7 that Xuan’s goal was to raise children who become productive adults.
“The reason he has all these children is because he wants them to contribute to society. He is not a man who is self-indulgent,” Krems said. “Some who are wealthy might spend on jewelry or cars, but he is actually spending his resources to help his children become educated so that they can be the philosophers, the physicians, the researchers and the inventors that help society.”
Krems did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment on Tuesday’s arrests.
Surrogacy is an arrangement in which a woman agrees to carry and deliver a child for another person or couple, often after an embryo transfer.
There is no comprehensive federal law regulating surrogacy, leaving most rules to the states.
California is considered a “surrogacy-friendly state” because it has clear laws governing the process. Both sides are required to have lawyers, and there must be a written, notarized contract before an embryo transfer takes place.
Investigators have said they were looking into whether the couple had misled surrogates around the country and that at least eight women came forward to say they were aggressively pursued by the couple to serve as surrogates.
The women, many of whom were first-time surrogates, say they were given misleading or incomplete information about the couple’s family situation and intentions.
At least one, Kayla Elliott, is now trying to get custody of a baby she birthed for the couple.

articles.title_orig: FSU brings entrepreneurship educators from around the world to Tallahassee for training
articles.title_zh: FSU brings entrepreneurship educators from around the world to Tallahassee for training
articles.content_orig:
Home / News / FSU Global / FSU brings entrepreneurship educators from around the world to Tallahassee for training
Florida State University welcomed entrepreneu r ship educators and leaders from around the world to Tallahassee last month for the 26th Experiential Classroom , an intensive professional development program designed to strengthen entrepreneurship educat ion .
Hosted by FSU’s Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship , this year’s program took place Sept. 17-19 and brought together participants from six countries, 21 U.S. states and Puerto Rico, representing 58 institutions and organizations. International participants came to Tallahassee from Canada, Ecuador, the Dominican Republic, Armenia and India.
The Experiential Classroom is housed at FSU and offered in partnership with the University of Notre Dame , the University of Tampa and the University of Florida . It was founded in 1999 by Michael Morris, a faculty member of the McKenna Center for Human Development and Global Business in the Keough School of Global Affairs at the University of Notre Dame.
The program has become a leading professional development experience for faculty, doctoral students, program directors and others seeking to strengthen how they teach entrepreneurship.
“The reach of this year’s Experiential Classroom speaks to the global leadership role Florida State’s Jim Moran College plays in entrepreneurship education,” said Michael Brady, interim dean of the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship. “We want FSU to be a destination not only for students who want to study entrepreneurship, but also for educators from around the world who want to become better at teaching it.”
While most participants came from colleges and universities, the cohort also included representatives from a high school and school district, as well as and community organizations such as the Chicago Urban League, mHUB and the Chicago Community Trust.
Unlike a traditional academic conference, the Experiential Classroom operates as an immersive teaching clinic. Participants learn alongside experienced entrepreneurship educators through classroom demonstrations, interactive sessions and hands-on exercises they can adapt to their own classrooms and entrepreneurship programs.
“The Experiential Classroom is about learning how to teach entrepreneurship by experiencing great entrepreneurship education,” said Susana Santos, Jim Moran Associate Professor of Entrepreneurship and co-director of the program. “Bringing together educators with different disciplinary, institutional and cultural perspectives creates an incredible learning environment. Participants leave with practical approaches they can immediately put to work and a global network of colleagues to rely on long after the clinic ends.”
The Experiential Classroom is part of FSU’s broader work to strengthen entrepreneurship education in the United States and abroad.
In 2025, Santos and Eric Liguori, Jim Moran Professor and associate dean for research and external relations in the college, traveled to Armenia with Vilma Fuentes, a visiting associate in research at FSU’s Learning Systems Institute , to train more than 30 faculty and administrators at the Armenian State University of Economics (ASUE) on contemporary approaches to entrepreneurship education.
The training was part of a U.S. Department of State-funded partnership designed to strengthen STEM and social entrepreneurship education and educational ties between the United States and Armenia. Liguori also regularly leads entrepreneurship educator development programs at universities across the United States, extending FSU’s expertise in experiential entrepreneurship education to faculty and institutions beyond the university’s campuses.
FSU’s work to advance entrepreneurship education internationally is also expanding through a strategic partnership with Universal AI University in Mumbai, India. Through the partnership, FSU faculty are working with their counterparts in India to help integrate entrepreneurship education into the university’s curriculum, bringing together FSU’s expertise in entrepreneurship education with Universal AI University’s focus on artificial intelligence and emerging technology.
FSU’s role as a hub for entrepreneurship education will be on display again Oct. 15-17, when the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship hosts the 2026 Global Consortium of Entrepreneurship Centers Annual Conference, bringing hundreds of university entrepreneurship leaders, educators and ecosystem builders from around the world to Tallahassee.
For more information about conference registration and sponsorship opportunities, visit the conference’s webpage . To learn more about the Jim Moran College of Entrepreneurship, visit jimmorancollege.fsu.edu .
To learn more about FSU’s global footprint, visit global.fsu.edu .

articles.title_zh: Ravens’ Marlon Humphrey, Tyler Loop among players joining Trump at Sparrows Point
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump visited Maryland on Tuesday to announce a project that's expected to support 14,000 jobs and become the state's largest job creator in over a decade.
The president toured Tradepoint Atlantic with Anduril Industries, a defense technology firm in Sparrows Point, and announced that the former Bethlehem Steel site will be turned into a 2-million-square-foot shipyard to build components for Virginia-class attack submarines.
According to a media briefing, the components include torpedo tubes, sterns and bow sections, and will be built at the Sparrows Point site.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore said this will be the largest private investment in the state in more than a decade.
"With this facility, thousands of Marylanders will have new pathways to work, wages, and wealth through advanced training and high-skilled maritime manufacturing jobs," said Moore. "We thank Anduril for choosing Maryland, and we're ready to build the future of the aerospace and defense economy together."
The facility is expected to support 14,000 jobs, including the creation of 3,100 permanent jobs. Over a decade, Arsenal-2, the name of the new industrial base, will become the state's largest job creator.
"For generations, this site shaped America's steel and shipbuilding legacy, including its critical role during World War II, when workers here built the vessels that helped defend our nation," Baltimore County Executive Kathy Klausmeier said in a statement.
The $3.7 billion private capital investment will become the largest single private investment in the state.
Happening right now, @realDonaldTrump has taken the stage in Sparrows Point to officially announce @anduriltech ’s new shipyard to help create the next generation of submarines for the @USNavy ! @wbaltv11 pic.twitter.com/EhDT4ohBt2
"With Arsenal-2, Anduril will return large-scale shipbuilding to a site that can once again define American naval power. This facility will make Baltimore County a critical part of America's submarine industrial base, adding the production capacity that the Navy needs to meet its Virginia-class requirements," said Brian Schimpf, Anduril cofounder and CEO.
Under the agreement, the state and Baltimore County will match up to 13% of the anticipated investment through existing economic incentive programs and new appropriations.
The state would also support the construction of a workforce training facility near Tradepoint Atlantic.

articles.title_zh: TOP FIVE STORYLINES: Sheldon Haudenschild’s Homecoming Sends World of Outlaws to Three Ohio Ovals
articles.content_orig:
October 6, 2026 at 3:04 pm
Sheldon Haudenschild cares deeply for his Ohio roots and continuing the state’s rich Sprint Car racing tradition.
The Wooster, OH native’s passion will be on display this weekend as he’s bringing the World of Outlaws NOS Energy Drink Sprint Car Series to his home state for a tripleheader at three different racetracks. Sheldon Haudenschild ’s NOS Energy Drink Buckeye Brawl Weekend sets the stage for a big trip to the “Buckeye State.” All three races will dish out $18,000 to the winner, a nod to Haudenschild’s car number with KCP Racing.
The brawl begins at Findlay, OH’s Millstream Speedway on Thursday, Oct. 8. The tour returned last year for the first time since 1994 and is back for a second consecutive season.
Round two takes The Greatest Show on Dirt to Mansfield Speedway on Friday, Oct. 9. Matt Tift and his team revived the historic track and are ready to welcome the World of Outlaws for the first time in 45 years.
The “Buckeye State” showcase is finalized on Saturday, Oct. 10, at Hartford, OH’s Sharon Speedway as the World of Outlaws makes its 16th stop at the northeast Ohio facility.
Let’s look at the top stories to watch this week:
The KCP Racing pit area will be busy all three nights this week.
Sheldon Haudenschild has amassed one of the most passionate followings in the sport, and it’s felt nowhere more than when he comes home. The Ohio fans watched his dad Jac Haudenschild ride the Haud Line to 72 World of Outlaws victories and many more accolades, and they’ve watched Sheldon follow in his footsteps in carving out his own legacy. He’s up to 55 career wins with nine of them coming this year, his first campaign with the KCP team.
Haudenschild would love nothing more than to add to that total this week. He’s won before at Millstream, topping a 2016 All Star Circuit of Champions (ASCoC) visit. Friday will mark his debut at Mansfield. He bagged a Sharon trophy with ASCoC in 2015 at the Lou Blaney Memorial . In World of Outlaws competition, he’s finished on the podium in four of his six tries. Sheldon Haudenschild has had this weekend circled on his calendar all year (Tyler Carr Photo)
David Gravel is closing in on history.
A rough stretch in California for the two-time opened the door for Michael “Buddy” Kofoid ’s championship hopes, but Gravel did his best to shut it as the scene shifted east. A win and a fourth at Williams Grove Speedway ’s National Open upped his point lead to 142 with just 10 races remaining. If he can hold on, he’ll join Steve Kinser, Donny Schatz , and Brad Sweet as only the fourth driver to ever claim three consecutive titles.
Don’t expect Gravel to stumble on Thursday as he enters Millstream as the defending winner at the Findlay, OH track. The Watertown, CT will make his first Mansfield laps the next night. He and Big Game Motorsports have been stellar at Sharon with a 2.8 average finish in six tries, highlighted by a 2024 triumph.
A trio of California-born World of Outlaws competitors ( Buddy Kofoid , Carson Macedo , and Cole Macedo ) consider Ohio a home away from home and look forward to any swing through the state. All three are united in the Linder family providing them a place to stay as they expanded their racing careers eastward.
Kofoid sits second in the standings heading to Ohio during his third tour with Roth Motorsports. His Millstream debut a year ago resulted in a runner-up finish. The time with the Linders led him to making one prior appearance at Mansfield, a fourth-place effort in 2019. He’s made four Sharon appearances, peaking at second last year.
Carson Macedo resides fourth in points, a manageable 32 markers back of Sheldon Haudenschild for third. His three trips to Millstream yielded a best finish of ninth last year in the Jason Johnson Racing No. 41. The Lemoore, CA native owns more Mansfield experience than most of his fellow World of Outlaws drivers with five starts leading to three podiums, including a 2018 Sprint Car World Championship prelim score. None of Macedo’s 10 Sharon Feature starts have resulted in a win, but he’s been on the podium on four occasions.
Cole Macedo’s sophomore World of Outlaws season sees him sitting eighth in the standings, which would mark a two-spot improvement over his rookie campaign if he can stay there. He took the TwoC Racing ride from 14th to seventh at Millstream last year. He’ll get his first look at Mansfield Saturday. Last year in his seventh Sharon appearance, the 26-year-old started on the pole and finished a solid sixth.
And speaking of Cole Macedo , he leads the most hotly contested battle in the points. Spots eight through 12 are separated by only 120 markers. The point fund and exclusivity bonus pay $70,000 more to finish eighth over 12th, so the five drivers in this fight will be scratching and clawing for every point they can get.
Behind Macedo, next in line is Spencer Bayston as his first year with Stenhouse Jr./Marshall Racing winds down. He won the season opener and has piled up 32 top 10s. He trails Macedo by 62.
Then it’s leading Kevin Gobrecht Rookie of the Year presented by Five Star Bodies contender Emerson Axsom 16 markers back of Bayston. Axsom and the Klaasmeyer/Petry Motorsports team have found some speed over the last couple months with 13 top 10s in 17 races, highlighted by Axsom’s first World of Outlaws win at Huset’s Speedway.
Only two points behind Axsom is Bill Balog . The “North Pole Nightmare” has dealt with several cases of bad luck recently, but his speed over that time suggests it wouldn’t be a surprise at all if the No. 17B breaks through into Victory Lane soon.
Rounding out the group is Series sophomore Chris Windom with 40 markers separating him from Balog. He got his first career victory in August at I-55 and picked up a pair of podiums last month in the Sides Motorsports No. 7S. Cole Macedo leads a hotly contested battle for eighth in the standings into Ohio (Tyler Carr Photo)
The World of Outlaws will have a group of talented “Buckeyes” ready to brawl this week with hopes of battling the best of the best for wins on the sport’s biggest stage.
Dale Blaney may only show up at Sharon, but he’s likely to make the most of that appearance. Last year he wheeled his brother Dave’s No. 10 to an extremely popular win at their home track, becoming the oldest victor in Series history at 61 years old.
Bradner, OH’s Nate Dussel has won at both Mansfield and Sharon this year. He’s topped a pair of FAST races at Mansfield and beat the ASCoC at Sharon in August.
Bellevue, OH’s Cap Henry is always one to watch when the World of Outlaws roll into his local region. He’s won nine 410 Sprint Car races in 2026, including Mansfield’s season opener in May.
These three will be joined by plenty more local gassers looking to impress under the bright lights.

articles.title_orig: Toyota shuts down rumors claiming that it’s ‘slashing prices’ in China
articles.title_zh: Toyota shuts down rumors claiming that it’s ‘slashing prices’ in China
articles.content_orig:
Toyota’s joint venture, FAW Toyota, issued a statement denying reports that it’s “slashing prices” in China and may exit the market entirely.
Toyota sells vehicles in China through two joint ventures: FAW Toyota and GAC Toyota. The long-standing joint ventures produce and sell Toyota models, including the Corolla, RAV4, and Avalon, as well as new electric vehicles like the bZ3 and bZ5.
Last week, on September 28, GAC Group announced plans to acquire a 50% stake in FAW Toyota. The plans include issuing new A-shares priced at 5.75 yuan per share.
Under the agreement, GAC said that FAW Group would become its second-largest shareholder, but exact details would be finalized following an audit and once the valuation work was complete.
FAW Toyota was established in 2000 as a joint venture between FAW Group and Toyota, with each holding a 50% share. It was initially called Tianjin FAW Toyota Motor Co until 2003, when it adopted the name FAW Toyota.
Once the agreement is finalized, GAC Group would take FAW’s 50% stake, while Toyota would retain the other 50%. GAC said the deal would not change the controller.
The move was widely viewed as part of Toyota’s efforts to revamp slumping brand sales in China and streamline operations.
Since the announcement, several reports have claimed that FAW Toyota plans to exit the market completely and is slashing prices to sell down inventory.
FAW Toyota issued a statement on Monday night, refuting the false claims. The company said:
In response to false statements circulating on certain online platforms —such as claims that “FAW Toyota may completely exit the market” and “Toyota is slashing prices”—our company reserves the right to pursue legal action.
The joint venture added that “the production, sales, and iterative development plans for all models are progressing smoothly as scheduled.”
Looking ahead, FAW Toyota will leverage the Group’s broader resources and technology for upcoming vehicles.
Toyota’s sales in China fell by 22.8% in August, marking the seventh straight month of lower sales due to weak demand for gas and hybrid models amid soaring fuel prices.

articles.title_orig: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.title_zh: Julie Jones makes history with silver at the World Archery 3D Championships
articles.content_orig:
YANKTON, S.D. – Julie Jones won silver at the World Archery 3D Championships, and in doing so created history by becoming the first USA woman to win an individual medal at the event, which began in 2003.
Jones was making only her second-ever appearance at the World Archery 3D Championships. She was part of the women’s team including Jayme Buchanan, Katherine Li and Madison Ritter to claim bronze at the 2024 World 3D Championships in Mokrice, Slovenia. Two years on and she did even better.
“It's a little surreal, I'll be honest,” began Julie Jones on hearing she had made history. “I love 3D. That is my passion aside from hunting. I guess if you ask me how I felt about it, I'm glad that I could bring it back for the U.S. team. But it really isn't a short answer. It goes a lot further than that.
"This whole time that I've been shooting, I've had an incredible team of people behind me from the very beginning. They have encouraged, they've pushed, they've believed in me when I had doubts about my own abilities. Without them, none of none of this would have been possible.
“I know that I don't have to prove anything to them but bringing this silver medal home, it's a testament to the training and the coaching that that I've received, that this medal belongs to all of these people, not just to me.”
Jones was seeded seventh after qualification before moving through the bracket with wins over teammate Mandy Boggs, Olga Timofeeva (RUS) and Martina Blahusova (CZE). The U.S. archer from Texas settled for silver after defeat in the gold medal match to fifth seed Judith Wenzl (GER).
“I had 100 percent confidence in the training and the coaching that I'd received," explained Jones. "I knew that if I applied all of the mental work, all of the physical work, as well as the actual shooting, I was reasonably confident that I could be in the top 10. That really wasn't a doubt in my mind.
"I knew that if I ran my process and executed well, that there was a good chance I would be in the top five, if not the top three. So that part of it was not necessarily a surprise to me.
“I've had some health challenges along the way and so day two was not a good day for me physically. And it was a struggle just to make it through the round. So that kind of threw a spanner into it.
“But I'm glad that it worked out as well as it did. I shoot very well under pressure. And I knew that if I could make it into those head-to-head eliminations, that I could work. Even though I had dropped points on day two, I knew that I could work myself back up to a to a better position.”
Julie Jones was also part of the bronze medal-winning traditional mixed team alongside Cody Hasson. Hasson, a double gold medalist at last year’s Pan American Field Championships, finished sixth in the individual men’s event.
Jones added, “I am tickled to death that Cody and I ended up with the bronze medal. He is a really, really strong shooter. I may be mistaken, but I don't think he's ever medaled before (at World 3D), and just to see the excitement and the absolute joy on his and our coach Shiloh's (Butts) face, when we realized that we had won that last round, that was a great feeling.”
For Jones, this was a family affair, with husband Daniel having also made the team. For Daniel, it was not only his World 3D Championship debut but also his first major event outside of local competition. A first major event for Daniel and the first U.S. woman to win an individual medal at the World 3D Championships for Julie. A case of keeping up with the Joneses!
“I'm just a normal person,” continued Julie. “I'm a mom. I have kids. I'm self-employed. I don't have a big, fancy facility, but, you know, I go out and I'm passionate about 3D archery.”
This success comes just a few weeks before a significant birthday for Julie on November 1. She said with a smile, “Just a month before, to achieve this, I couldn’t ask for anything more. This is year 50 for me. I have my 50th birthday coming up. And winning individual silver is pretty much the best present that I could imagine.”
Matt Hudson and Ava Jones combined to take silver in the barebow mixed team. Seeded at number two, the pair defeated Austria (150-136) and Denmark (152-141) before defeat to Russia (144-123). Ava Jones, making her World Archery 3D Championships debut, came in fourth in barebow women.
Other top 10 individual finishes came for Kim Timberlake (4th in longbow women), Joella Bates (8th in longbow women) and Lee Wilkins (10th in longbow men). Timberlake’s march to the bronze medal match included a 96-66 quarterfinals win over third seed Paula Virmasalo (FIN).

China represents just 3% of Walmart’s business. But the market is fast-growing—and in charge of that growth is Christina Zhu, the president and CEO of Walmart China.
Zhu is one of the execs featured on Fortune’s new Most Powerful Women Asia list , published today. She comes in at No. 19 for her role running a $24.6 billion business that has grown 19% year-over-year.
My colleague Nicholas Gordon writes about Zhu’s tenure in the role and Walmart’s history in China in a new feature . Walmart entered China in 1996. Today, its success comes from a few strategies to meet the high expectations of the Chinese shopper: extreme convenience, in the form of lightning-fast delivery, and an “in-person shopping experience so novel that stores have become vacation destinations for shoppers throughout the region.” In China, Sam’s Club is bigger than Walmart’s namesake retailer. Shoppers show up to buy in bulk items including gift boxes of mooncakes and abalone for the Mid-Autumn Festival.
Other execs who make this year’s MPW Asia list include repeat No. 1 Tan Su Shan, who leads the Singapore-based bank DBS Group and familiar faces like Canva’s Melanie Perkins and Huawei’s Meng Wanzhou, who all appeared on our 2026 global MPW list .

articles.title_orig: Bellingham man charged in connection to February school shooting in British Columbia
articles.title_zh: Bellingham man charged in connection to February school shooting in British Columbia
articles.content_orig:
US authorities have announced the arrest of a 30-year-old from Washington state in connection with the February school shooting in Tumbler Ridge, British Columbia.
The person, identified by authorities as James Cody Bryant, was arrested in Bellingham, Washington, on Tuesday morning on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country, according to an announcement by the US Justice Department. The February attack on a secondary school in the small town of Tumbler Ridge was Canada’s deadliest school shooting in decades, leaving eight people dead and dozens wounded.
Bryant was scheduled to appear in court Tuesday afternoon in Seattle, according to a press release ahead of the announcement. CNN has not yet confirmed whether Bryant has legal representation.
Bryant was allegedly “in repeated contact with” the 18-year-old Canadian shooter, Jesse Van Rootselaar, “offering advice, sending money, and even agreeing to live stream the horrific event” on Twitch, said Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, at a press conference in Seattle.
The money amounted to a little over $100, primarily to buy a lighter and a pair of shoes that Van Rootselaar “wanted to have when she conducted this killing spree,” Floyd said. The two discussed sending weapons to Van Rootselaar, but ultimately Bryant was uncomfortable with doing so, authorities alleged.
Bryant began an online friendship with Van Rootselaar after meeting on video chatting website Omegle three years before the shooting, authorities said. After Van Rootselaar killed two family members, Bryant allegedly offered the attacker advice on how to fix a car when it failed to start en route to the school.
Canadian and US authorities have said that Bryant and Van Rootselaar, who died in the shooting, are trans women, though officials used male and female pronouns interchangeably to describe the two throughout the press conference.
Assistant Commissioner Elija Rain of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police said Canadian authorities contacted the US Department of Homeland Security soon after the shooting, based on “information from one of the online platforms used by the shooter.”
“As further alleged, instead of de-escalating or reporting to law enforcement, Bryant continued to enable the shooter over the months they discussed these plans,” said FBI agent Mike Harrington. “In addition to providing money, technical advice and particular items to be used in the shooting, Bryant agreed to record a live stream feed of the attack and broadcast it in a way that would maximize notoriety for the shooter.”
It was not previously known that anyone apart from Van Rootselaar allegedly participated in planning the massacre.
Seven families of victims sued tech company OpenAI in April after information emerged that the shooter had used ChatGPT to plan the attack. The week before the suit was filed, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman apologized to the community for not alerting law enforcement after Van Rootselaar’s account was banned.
CNN’s Josh Campbell and Paula Newton contributed reporting. This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: The most ambitious ideas to save the world from El Niño
articles.title_zh: The most ambitious ideas to save the world from El Niño
articles.content_orig:
Countries around the world are bracing for a torrid few months as the El Niño weather phenomenon looks set to wreak havoc on shorelines, farmland and ocean ecosystems.
Already, India is grappling with the impacts of one of the driest monsoon seasons on record. Meanwhile, in Indonesia, schools have closed and authorities have advised residents to stay indoors to avoid the toxic smoke from huge wildfires supercharged by El Niño .
But what if we could take the sting out of the tail of El Niño – or even stop it from happening altogether? That’s the hope of physicists, chemists and engineers working on ideas ranging from the outrageously radical to the just-might-work.
One of the most ambitious ideas for halting El Niño is to repurpose a technique called artificial upwelling that was initially conceived to boost the uptake of carbon by the oceans. This form of geoengineering involves pumping cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean up to the surface to encourage the growth of plankton, which would then absorb and store carbon from the atmosphere.
Katharine Ricke at the University of California, San Diego, says artificial upwelling could be used to cool sea-surface temperatures in the tropical Pacific, potentially preventing an El Niño from forming .
Explainer: What is El Niño?
But – and it is a big but – the technical feasibility of deploying artificial upwelling on this scale would be a “major, major undertaking”, she says. Ricke has previously investigated whether the approach could be used to cool sea-surface temperatures in the Indian Ocean and found it would require approximately 5.8 million kilometres of pipe, nearly double the total length of all pipelines in the world.
There is also the problem that nobody knows what putting that amount of pipework into the ocean would do to other marine life. “The ecosystem effects of installing ocean pipes at that scale are really not well understood at all,” she says.
Another equally ambitious, but perhaps more promising, approach for preventing El Niño could be to use another geoengineering technique called marine cloud brightening.
The El Niño climate phase occurs when easterly winds weaken, allowing warm water built up in the western Pacific to slosh back across the central and eastern parts of the ocean. Spraying droplets of seawater into the air below low-lying stratocumulus clouds in the Pacific would increase their brightness, reflecting more sunlight back to space. This would then bring down sea-surface temperatures, strengthening trade winds to blow warm water back into the western Pacific and reverse the El Niño pattern.
A study published in July, co-authored by Ricke, concluded that deploying marine cloud brightening in this way would dramatically reduce the strength of an El Niño and push the system back into a neutral state much earlier than normal.
Why is this monster El Niño so strong?
This won’t come in time to prevent the current El Niño, says Jessica Wan at the University of Chicago, a co-author of the research. The technology needed to brighten clouds on this scale doesn’t exist, plus there is no international framework for countries to agree this kind of geoengineering intervention. “It’s not something we could implement for this El Niño or maybe even the next one,” says Wan.
So, for now at least, El Niño cycles aren’t going anywhere – but can we make them more tolerable?
One particularly devastating consequence of the way El Niño turns up the global temperature dial and shifts rain patterns around the world is that it threatens food supplies. The United Nations World Food Programme estimates that 274 million people in 45 countries will be acutely food insecure by the end of 2027, 49 million more than today.
Work is under way to develop new breeds of crops capable of withstanding the extreme conditions brought about with El Niño. Rice is a particular priority, says Erik Murchie at the University of Nottingham in the UK.
Murchie is part of a team developing heat-tolerant rice varieties, with trials now ongoing in the Philippines. This is part of a global effort: in 2025, researchers in China reported the discovery of a gene variant that can preserve yield and rice quality during hot nights, one of the major threats to rice yields. Gene-editing or selective breeding could allow this trait in commercial crops, the team says, with the field trials indicating a 31 to 78 per cent greater yield under high temperatures compared with standard rice strains.
Such a goal isn’t a fantasy – in the 1990s, scientists pinpointed a rice gene that allows a traditional rice variety known as FR13A to survive a week of submergence in flood water. The SUB1 gene has since been introduced into several major rice varieties around the world, making crops more resilient to climate-driven flood risks.
Housing, people and infrastructure are also vulnerable to rising water levels and flooding driven by El Niño. Traditional flood-protection measures are already being deployed, from coastal barricades to temporary barriers. In California, drains are being cleared and sandbags handed out, while residents are being urged to prepare their properties for high winds and flood risk.
But one company has a more drastic idea to protect against flood risk more permanently: raising the height of land. California start-up Terranova has developed a robot that injects a mix of wood slurry into the ground, raising the height of land at risk of flooding from sea-level rise.
The robots drill wells around 12 to 18 metres deep into the ground and then inject the mix, made from wood waste, into the earth. The robotic system can lift up a roughly 4000-square-metre area by about 30 centimetres per day, the firm says.  “We’re combining heavy robotics and geotechnical innovation to literally reshape the world,” the firm’s CEO Laurence Allen said in a 2025 statement announcing $7 million of venture capital investment.
However, Nigel Wright at the University of Birmingham in the UK says extensive testing should be done before deploying the technology at a large scale. He queries whether the wood waste would solidify, remain as slurry or decompose underground over the long term. “I would question whether the soil structure would be stable enough over 20 or 30 years to actually support houses,” he says.
Inside the oceans, coral reefs are on the front line of the El Niño crisis. Elevated ocean temperatures caused by El Niño can cause mass coral-bleaching events, in which corals expel the symbiotic algae living in their tissues. This process can severely stress, and ultimately kill, corals.
Shading corals could help. One test of the approach is happening this month: five floating hexagons that block harmful ultraviolet rays are being installed in a small coral nursery in Florida. The plan is to extend this to 100 shading units in June next year, which will be distributed among restoration organisations working across Florida to test their effectiveness at protecting corals and any impact on the long-term health of the ecosystem.
In Australia, an approach that goes even further has been tested. Greg Qiao at the University of Melbourne set out more than a decade ago to create a chemical film that would sit atop agricultural reservoirs to minimise water loss to evaporation. After extensive trials, that idea never came to fruition – but Qiao realised the work could be repurposed for coral reefs.
The aim for a coral reef is to block sunlight, rather than prevent evaporation, so Qiao’s team developed a thin film layer made from calcium carbonate coated with stearic acid. The layer is one molecule thick and designed to sit on the surface of the ocean above a reef. Field trials in 2018 suggested the film reduced light hitting the corals by 30 per cent. “That’s probably enough for us to stop the bleach,” says Qiao. articles.title_orig: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.title_zh: U.K. Security Adviser Traveled to Israel Ahead of Consulate Closure
articles.content_orig:
The UK government is making a last-ditch attempt to persuade Israel not to close the British consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.
Israel said in September that it would shut the mission, which is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv, in retaliation for the UK announcing sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
British sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.
The Foreign Office said it would not comment on "speculation and live discussions" that the UK could expel Israeli diplomats in response.
The Israeli government said it would close the mission within 30 days of the UK sanctions announcement, meaning that the mission - first established in 1838 - will close on Thursday unless a deal is reached.
The consulate handles UK relations with Palestinians in the city as well as in the West Bank and Gaza.
UK National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell made an undisclosed visit to Israel last week for talks but seemingly left without reaching an agreement.
According to Israeli media, the UK is threatening to expel up to 27 Israeli diplomats if the closure goes ahead.
Such a tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats is more common among adversaries than allies.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's PM programme, former British ambassador to Israel, Matthew Gould, said any decision by the UK to expel Israeli diplomats would inflict "grievous damage" on the relationship between both countries.
He said areas affected could include defence, security and technology.
Gould told the programme: "When you've got to a stage where you are chucking out the big majority of Israeli diplomats in London, I don't think that's purely symbolic.
"I think at that point you're doing really quite serious damage to the structure and the substructure of the relationship."
He added that governments "have a choice", that the expulsion of Israeli diplomats would be a "gift to the Israeli right", and would help Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu win re-election.
France and Canada joined the UK in the initial sanctions, but Israel has not taken action against them.
Emily Thornberry, chair of the foreign affairs committee, said: "Beyond the fact that the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem - occupied Palestinian territory - is not in Israel's prerogative, it is yet another attempt by this far-right Israeli government to block a two-state solution."
She added: "It is illegal, and the UK must resist it."
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has previously said that they do not want the consulate to close.
"It would damage the very important work that we are doing, helping people in those communities," he said last month.

A variant of the H1N1 influenza virus is dominating flu season in the Northern Hemisphere so far this year. Shown here are H1N1 influenza virus particles (yellow) releasing from an infected lung cell (green). Credit: Science Photo Library
Data show that flu season in the Northern Hemisphere might be off to an early start — prompting a rethink about when people should get their annual vaccines against the influenza virus . The percentage of positive tests for influenza is unusually high for this time of the year in places such as the United Kingdom and on the West Coast of the United States (see ‘Surprising start’). In Japan, outbreaks in August and early September forced some schools to close just as they were starting back up after the summer break.
“It would be an incredibly early season” for the United States if the cases researchers are seeing on the West Coast continue to rise at their current rate, says Scott Hensley, a virologist at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia.
The influenza subtype responsible for most of the US cases so far is H1N1, in a flip from last year, when H3N2 dominated. And sequencing data from these early cases point to an emerging mutation in H1N1 that is causing concern among specialists.
Source: Adapted from US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data
These findings come from a relatively small number of positive tests compared with those available during peak flu season, so it’s too soon to predict the overall trajectory of the outbreak, researchers say. “An early start doesn’t necessarily mean a more severe season,” says James Hay, an epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, UK. Still, “there is something afoot”, wrote epidemiologist Caitlin Rivers in her newsletter, ‘Force of Infection’, on 27 September .
It’s enough to make Rivers, who is a researcher at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore, Maryland, reconsider her personal protection strategy. In a typical year, when flu season peaks in December and January in the United States, she would wait until mid-to-late October for a shot, to get the best protection. Now, she’s thinking about getting a jab as soon as possible.
Seasonal flu is usually caused by some combination of three viruses: two subtypes of influenza A — H3N2 and H1N1 — and influenza B. Because influenza viruses genetically mutate over time and people’s immunity alters as they get vaccines and infections, which of the three viruses emerges as dominant changes for each flu season. US data showed that, during the week ending on 26 September, H1N1 accounted for 96% of positive cases for which subtyping was performed. H3N2 accounted for almost 4% of cases, and influenza B wasn’t detected.
That’s in contrast to last year, when a new variant of H3N2, called subclade K, emerged. It became globally dominant because it had many mutations that made people more vulnerable to it.

This year, the H1N1 mutation that is worrying researchers is G155E. Alex Greninger, a virologist at the University of Washington in Seattle, says that his laboratory detected G155E in 13 of 17 H1N1 samples taken from people in whom the genetic sequences were complete enough to identify specific mutations. The samples had come from hospitals and clinics in Seattle over the past few months.
This mutation had already been flagged in an analysis led by Jesse Bloom, a virologist at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center in Seattle, which was posted on the preprint server bioRxiv last month, ahead of peer review 1 .
Bloom and his colleagues tested how well antibodies in blood samples from 260 people in Australia and the United States were able to recognize and block infection from 148 influenza A viruses circulating by mid-2026. “We saw that a number of strains which have the G155E mutation are, in some cases, less well recognized by pre-existing human antibodies,” Bloom says. Antibodies in serum from teenagers and young adults were especially inept at recognizing this variant, probably because many in these groups haven’t been exposed to H1N1 viruses with similar characteristics before .

articles.title_orig: China's $100M Gaza Pledge: Beijing Hasn't Said What's Spent
articles.title_zh: China's $100M Gaza Pledge: Beijing Hasn't Said What's Spent
articles.content_orig:
Choose your language to begin.
Nine months after Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged $100 million to ease the crisis in Gaza, Beijing has not said how much of it has been spent. When Sun Zhen, who heads China’s diplomatic office to the Palestinians, announced new aid at a Sept. 29 reception in Ramallah — urgent cash support for the Palestinian Authority and three more tranches through UNICEF, the U.N. Development Programme and the Egyptian Red Crescent — he gave no amounts but said the details are still being coordinated.
Palestinian Economy Minister Mohammed Al-Amour attended on behalf of President Mahmoud Abbas. The Chinese office’s English readout said only that Sun “outlined China’s assistance to Palestine.” The details came from Palestinian media .
Sun highlighted that China, working with UNICEF, has already delivered winter clothing and medical supplies to more than 38,000 children in Gaza and medicines to six health facilities. That is a small share of Gaza’s roughly 1.1 million children, according to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics . China reported the Gaza deliveries by the number of people helped, not by cost, making a comparison between the $100 million pledge and other donors’ spending difficult.
The $100 million was always modest. In April 2025, the EU announced up to €1.6 billion ($1.8 billion) for the Palestinians over three years, including €620 million ($697 million) in grants to the Palestinian Authority.
All of that pales compared with Gaza’s immense need. A U.N. damage and needs assessment , released in April 2026, put the cost to rebuild and rehabilitate Gaza at $71.4 billion over the next decade.
China’s longer-term footprint is even smaller. MBN’s China Tracker monitors projects across the Middle East and North Africa under the Belt and Road Initiative, Beijing’s global infrastructure and investment program. It records four in the Palestinian territories since 2023, all in or near Ramallah: a Chinese school, a Friendship Square, an 11-kilometer extension of Beijing Road, and the Friendship and Development Building signed this September, which Chinese officials call their largest aid project in Palestine.
“China’s primary interests in Gaza are currently political and strategic rather than commercial,” Mordechai Chaziza, an associate professor at Ashkelon Academic College in Israel who studies China’s role in the Middle East, told MBN via email. “Beijing seeks to strengthen its image as a supporter of the Palestinian cause, reinforce its role as an alternative diplomatic actor in the Middle East, and challenge the perception that the United States is the only external power capable of shaping regional outcomes.”
That approach also shows in reconstruction, where China has stood alone. On Sept. 23, the U.S.-backed Board of Peace, chaired by U.S. President Donald Trump and set up to oversee Gaza’s postwar rebuilding, unveiled a $2.45 billion , six-month plan of 66 projects. The board’s high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, said the plan depends on Hamas disarming.
China was invited to join the board in January, but it has not said whether it will, saying only that it backs a U.N.-centered system. Staying outside “may limit China’s direct influence over reconstruction decisions,” Chaziza said. But working through Egypt, Arab states and Palestinian institutions lets Beijing keep influence “while avoiding the political and financial risks associated with leading the reconstruction process.”
China’s presence is most concrete in supplies. MBN confirmed in U.N. records that the Chinese company Haike was awarded a standing U.N. supply agreement in April 2025 for mobile homes in Gaza. The agreement sets no quantity or value, so it guarantees no sales. The Israeli business paper Globes reported that Haike won the contract with a bid 50 to 60 percent below the runner-up, and that a Chinese firm was among the lowest bidders on a later U.N. Development Programme contract for 45,000 homes. MBN could not independently verify the bid figures.
Chinese companies have the technical capacity and experience to take part in Gaza’s reconstruction, Chaziza said, but how big a role they play “will depend less on economic capability and more on political arrangements.”
If reconstruction runs through “Western-backed institutions with strict procurement conditions, Chinese firms may face limitations,” he said. If Arab states and international organizations take a more inclusive approach, Chinese companies “could become important participants.”
The test is what comes next: whether the cash and the three tranches arrive, at what value, who wins the Gaza contracts and whether Beijing ever engages with the Board of Peace.
“China’s goal is not to replace the United States in Gaza,” Chaziza said, “but to expand its political influence by presenting itself as a supporter of Palestinian rights, a partner of Arab states, and a potential contributor to reconstruction while protecting its broader regional interests.”

articles.title_zh: Idaho sets new Guinness World Record for largest serving of French fries

Live updates all day, breaking news as it happens and weather every 10 minutes
Idaho is now home to a new Guinness World Records title after a team served up more than 1,400 pounds of french fries in Boise.
Click here for updates on this story
SOUTHEAST BOISE, Idaho ( KIVI ) -- Idaho is now home to a new Guinness World Records title after the Idaho Potato Commission and Spud Daddy served up more than 1,400 pounds of French fries Friday night.
The team was attempting to beat the previous record for the largest serving of French fries, which stood at 1,452.85 pounds and was set in India in 2018.
“Idaho should have that record,” Thomas Watson with Spud Daddy said. “Idaho doesn’t have that record, and it’s our mission to bring the record home.”
The attempt took plenty of preparation and a large group of volunteers.
Watson said about 50 to 60 people helped cut and flash-freeze the potatoes before they were loaded into a refrigerated truck and eventually fried for the final attempt.
“It’s been awesome just to see it,” Watson said.
About 1,700 pounds of raw Idaho potatoes went into the effort.
After the fries were cooked and weighed, the final total came in at 1,474 pounds — more than 20 pounds above the previous record.
That made Idaho the new Guinness World Records holder for the largest serving of French fries.
The record attempt was part of Potato Days at the Idaho Botanical Garden, a family-friendly event celebrating Idaho's potato industry and the farmers, packers, distributors and retailers behind it.
The event also featured the Big Idaho Potato Truck, live music, lawn games and plenty of potato-based food, including fries, tots, mashed potatoes, loaded baked potatoes and potato soup.
After the record was officially set, Watson said he was ready to finally relax.
“I’m ready to take a nap,” Watson said. “I’m going to be so excited that this thing we have been thinking about is now done. We can go to sleep. We can get some food. We can eat some French fries.”

articles.title_zh: CIA officer arrested with gold bars admits he exposed secret intelligence source to a foreign official

BREAKING: Christa Pike is awake and speaking after surviving a failed execution attempt in Tennessee, her lawyers say
ALEXANDRIA, Virginia — A high-ranking CIA officer arrested after federal agents found roughly 600 pounds of gold bars stashed in his home also disclosed details about a secret U.S. intelligence source to a foreign official, prosecutors said Tuesday during his plea hearing.
David Rush, 49, admitted to one count of wire fraud under an agreement with federal prosecutors and faces up to 20 years in prison when he is sentenced Jan. 28.
Justice Department officials said Rush siphoned off $194 million in government funds, using his position at the CIA to create an elaborate scheme designed to facilitate his “maximum self-enrichment at the expense of the United States.”
In a plea document , Rush admitted that in late 2025 he disclosed “certain descriptive information of a U.S. government clandestine human source” that could “endanger the safety and life of the human source and the U.S. government officers working with the source,” as well as jeopardize America’s “ability to recruit human sources, who rely on the U.S. government’s assurance of absolute secrecy.”
Lawyers for Rush declined to comment.
Rush has been in jail since his arrest May 19, after investigators said he made up details about his education and military service record, fooling the nation’s top spy agency for years.
As a top officer at the CIA’s Directorate of Science and Technology, Rush had access to the nation’s most secret programs -- and he used that to his benefit, prosecutors said. Rush worked as a liaison to the Pentagon for sensitive military programs and collaborated closely with the Defense Department’s powerful second in command , Steve Feinberg, people familiar with the work have told NBC News.
The case has prompted a wave of shock and anxiety among lawmakers and within the insular spy agency. How could someone have fooled the highest levels of government for decades, and how could he have gotten through what is considered a rigorous vetting process to join the CIA? The intelligence community’s watchdog is separately investigating, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the probe.
Until Tuesday, Rush — who was placed on leave sometime before his arrest and then fired — had only formally been charged with one count of theft of public funds, accused of falsifying his pay records. His court case was postponed for weeks as his lawyers and the government worked toward a possible plea agreement . U.S. District Judge Michael Nachmanoff approved the plea deal Tuesday.
Rush acted alone, using his manufactured bona fides to create confidence in his work, court documents say. No other CIA officials, government employees or contractors were accused of crimes in the case. According to court documents, his deceptions “caused contractors and subcontractors to carry out the transactions”
Rush fabricated a highly classified program to funnel tens millions of dollars for his personal purchase of luxury real estate in Florida and invented a sensitive government “activity” to acquire the gold bars.
“Rush effectively acted as his own approving official, enabling him to expend substantial amounts of United States government money without meaningful scrutiny,” according to court documents.
During their search of his home, investigators seized about 300 gold bars, federal officials said , along with about $2 million in U.S. currency and 35 luxury watches. Initially, investigators said it was 303 bars, but on Tuesday revised that figure to 298 bars.
The gold was for what Rush claimed was an official work purpose, and he had said that they were distributed out -- the spy agency uses all sorts of unusual methods in its work.
Rush, according to federal prosecutors, also fabricated a classified special access program, and told associates he needed luxury real estate in South Florida for it. He had $145 million transferred to a holding company for four luxury properties and vehicles.
He lied to associates, telling them that highly-placed government officials knew about the need for the real estate and approved the transaction.
Rush also spent $1.8 million of the government’s money for private charter flights, but a CIA review later found he had “no legitimate official requirement” for these flights, prosecutors said.
The interstate wire fraud occurred in January — when Rush caused a government employee to send $45 million for his scheme, prosecutors said.
The case also has cast a spotlight on Rush’s relationship with Feinberg, as NBC News reported . The FBI reviewed video showing Rush and Feinberg at a residence in the Washington region that is linked to the federal government, according to four people familiar with the video.
Feinberg has been interviewed by the FBI, according to two people familiar with the investigation , but has not been accused of any wrongdoing, and the bureau said he is not under investigation. There’s no indication that Feinberg knew of Rush’s alleged fabrications. A Pentagon spokesman has said Feinberg and Rush were not close.
CIA Director John Ratcliffe said in a statement Tuesday that the agency “immediately” referred to case to the FBI after an internal investigation identified potential crimes, and said Rush “abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions.”
FBI Director Kash Patel said Rush “betrayed his oath, his co-workers, and the American people” when he “defrauded the government of hundreds of millions of dollars, and then misused those funds for extravagant purchases.”
Gary Grumbach is an NBC News legal affairs reporter, based in Washington, D.C.

articles.title_zh: Cornell brings in ex-Justice official Sally Yates to review school’s handling of sex assault claims
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of people gathered at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Monday in support of "Jane Doe," the former student who alleges she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a fraternity in October 2024.
The "Justice for Survivors" rally was organized by over 20 student organizations who led a late afternoon march to Day Hall, which houses the university's administrative offices and had been vandalized by activists overnight .
Students, faculty, and residents from across the state took part in the protest calling for Cornell administrators to resign over their handling of the case.
"We are known as the rape school," Saya Taylor, a Cornell sophomore, said at the rally. "We can be known as leading a nationwide reform movement."
Demonstrators held signs accusing the Ivy League school of protecting the alleged rapists and demanding accountability.
"Jane Doe deserved a campus that supported her," Taylor said. "Jane Doe deserved an administration that delivered a fair and proper judicial process. Jane Doe deserved a police department that would actually follow up on her case. Instead, she was silenced."
Late Monday, the Cornell University faculty introduced a resolution declaring it has no confidence in the administration's ability to address the "ongoing crisis of sexual assault" on campus. According to NBC News , the proposal is expected to be considered by the Faculty Senate on Oct. 14.
"The goal is to really force systemic change," Faculty Senator Paul Ortiz said in a statement to NBC. "Women need to feel safe."
On Monday night, Cornell University President Michael Kotlikoff and Ryan Lombardi, the school's vice president for student and campus life, met with the Graduate and Professional Student Assembly, which pressed them on their response to Jane Doe's allegations.
Cornell students participate in a protest over the university's handling of the "Jane Doe" case on Oct. 5.
"We're all angry. I understand that anger," Kotlikoff said, according to the Cornell Daily Sun . "People want easy answers to this."
He added: "This passion, if appropriately channeled, can help us as a community address this issue."
On Tuesday, Cornell's board of trustees announced it has retained former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates, a partner at law firm King & Spalding, to lead an independent review of how the university responds to sexual assault on campus.
"As part of that broader mandate, Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the University's response to the allegations involving Jane Doe and members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter," the board of trustees said in a statement .
The developments came hours after audio of a phone call between Jane Doe and one of the accused fraternity members, recorded weeks after the alleged incident, was released by ABC News . During the call, Jane Doe said she was "10 shots deep" when she arrived at the Chi Phi fraternity house and was now struggling to remember what had caused "so much damage on my body and brain."
"The only way for me to heal is to know what happened," she said. "That's why I'm trying to just piece it together, you know, like I'm just like confused."
The fraternity member told her that she consented to having a threesome with him and another fraternity brother.  He also insisted that Jane Doe had told him she had not been drinking when she showed up.
"You did tell me you were sober, by the way," he said. "You said you hadn't been anywhere."
"That is not true. I never would have said that," she replied.
The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., on Oct. 1.
At one point during the Nov. 7, 2024, call, Jane Doe told him, "If I wanted to take this somewhere, what y'all did would be classified as gang rape."
The fraternity member then suggested that their memory of what transpired may be inaccurate.
"I have racked my brain for this mystery," he said. "You know, it's possible that both of us, like, remember this, and it's not true."
Jane Doe pushed back: "No, because I remember looking up and being like, 'That is too many people.'"
